item.title: “Monks, these nine perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What…
item.description:
“Monks, these nine perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end. What nine? The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of not-self in suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion. These nine perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as their end.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.16

item.title: “And how, monks, is a monk one who has completely cut off all searches? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the search for sensual pleasures,…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is a monk one who has completely cut off all searches? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the search for sensual pleasures, abandoned the search for existence, and the search for the holy life has been calmed. Thus, monks, is a monk who has completely cut off all searches. And how, monks, is a monk one whose thoughts are unblemished? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned sensual thought, abandoned ill-will thought, abandoned harmful thought. Thus, monks, is a monk whose thoughts are unblemished. And how, monks, is a monk one whose mental activities are calmed? Here, monks, a monk, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, with the previous passing away of joy and grief, enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, neither painful nor pleasant, with equanimity and mindfulness purified. Thus, monks, is a monk whose mental activities are calmed. And how, monks, is a monk one whose mind is well liberated? Here, monks, a monk’s mind is liberated from greed, liberated from hatred, liberated from delusion. Thus, monks, is a monk whose mind is well liberated. And how, monks, is a monk one whose wisdom is well liberated? Here, monks, a monk knows: ‘Greed has been abandoned in me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, unable to arise in the future’; knows: ‘Hatred has been abandoned in me …’; knows: ‘Delusion has been abandoned in me, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, unable to arise in the future.’ Thus, monks, is a monk whose wisdom is well liberated. Monks, all those noble ones in the past who lived the noble dwelling — they lived these ten noble dwellings. All those noble ones in the future who will live the noble dwelling — they will live these ten noble dwellings. All those noble ones in the present who live the noble dwelling — they live these ten noble dwellings. These, monks, are the ten noble dwellings that the noble ones have lived, are living, and will live.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.20
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are tied, infatuated, utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who do not see their peril, who…
item.description:
“Monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are tied, infatuated, utterly committed to these five strands of sensual pleasure, who do not see their peril, who do not know the escape from them, and who enjoy them—they should be understood as having fallen into misfortune, into calamity, and are being used by Māra as he wishes. Monks, just as a forest deer that has fallen into a trap must lie down—that deer should be understood as having fallen into misfortune, into calamity, and is being used by the hunter as he wishes. When the hunter comes, the deer cannot leave as it wishes. So too, monks, those ascetics or brahmins who are tied … are being used by Māra as he wishes.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta

item.title: “Householder, suppose there is a hungry, weak dog at a slaughterhouse. A skilled butcher or his apprentice throws it a bone that has been well-scraped,…
item.description:
“Householder, suppose there is a hungry, weak dog at a slaughterhouse. A skilled butcher or his apprentice throws it a bone that has been well-scraped, thoroughly scraped, with no meat left, only smeared with blood. What do you think, householder? Would that dog, by gnawing on that bone — well-scraped, thoroughly scraped, with no meat, only smeared with blood — be able to dispel its hunger and weakness?” “No, venerable sir. Why is that? Because that bone is well-scraped, thoroughly scraped, with no meat, only smeared with blood; the dog would only get weary and distressed.” “So too, householder, a noble disciple reflects: ‘The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are like a bone — of much suffering, much despair, and the peril is even greater.’ Having seen this as it actually is with perfect wisdom, having abandoned the equanimity based on diversity, dependent on diversity, and having cultivated the equanimity based on unity, dependent on unity, where all clinging to the world’s materials is completely abandoned without remainder, he cultivates such equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 54 – Potaliyasutta

item.title: “Monks, here a clansman, abandoning sensual pleasures, goes forth from the household life into homelessness. But because of those sensual pleasures, or other sensual pleasures…
item.description:
“Monks, here a clansman, abandoning sensual pleasures, goes forth from the household life into homelessness. But because of those sensual pleasures, or other sensual pleasures worse than those, he is destroyed, ruined, falls, lies prostrate. These five hindrances, monks, are obscurations, hindrances, coverings of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. What five? Sensual desire, monks, is an obscuration, a hindrance, a covering of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. Ill-will … sloth and torpor … restlessness and remorse … doubt, monks, is an obscuration, a hindrance, a covering of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. These five hindrances, monks, are obscurations, hindrances, coverings of the mind, debilitating to wisdom. The seven factors of enlightenment, monks, are not obscurations, not hindrances, not coverings of the mind; when developed and cultivated, they lead to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation. What seven? The mindfulness factor of enlightenment … The equanimity factor of enlightenment — these are not obscurations, not hindrances, not coverings of the mind; when developed and cultivated, they lead to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.39
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “‘The world is deficient, longing, a slave to craving’ — that, great king, is the fourth exposition of the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One,…
item.description:
“‘The world is deficient, longing, a slave to craving’ — that, great king, is the fourth exposition of the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, the Knower, the Seer, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having known, seen, and heard that exposition, I went forth from the household life into homelessness.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta

item.title: “Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, thought: ‘This Dhamma that I have realized is deep, hard to see, hard to…
item.description:
“Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, thought: ‘This Dhamma that I have realized is deep, hard to see, hard to awaken to, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of logic, subtle, to be understood by the wise. But this generation delights in sensual pleasures, is devoted to sensual pleasures, is fond of sensual pleasures. For a generation that delights in sensual pleasures, is devoted to sensual pleasures, is fond of sensual pleasures, it is hard to see this principle of specific conditionality (dependent origination); it is hard to see the principle that all formations are peaceful, that all substrates of rebirth are eliminated, that craving is destroyed, that there is dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 14 – Mahāpadānasutta

item.title: “I do not see any other form, monks, that so obsesses and occupies the mind of a man as the form of a woman. The…
item.description:
“I do not see any other form, monks, that so obsesses and occupies the mind of a man as the form of a woman. The form of a woman, monks, obsesses and occupies the mind of a man.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.1

item.title: Elder Parāpariya: “Having abandoned the six sense-bases, With sense-doors well restrained, Having pulled out the root of evil, I have attained the destruction of defilements.”
item.description:
Elder Parāpariya:
“Having abandoned the six sense-bases,
With sense-doors well restrained,
Having pulled out the root of evil,
I have attained the destruction of defilements.”

From: Theragāthā 1.116

item.title: Elder Tissa: “As if struck by a sword, As if his head were on fire, Mindful, a monk should go forth, Abandoning sensual lust.”
item.description:
Elder Tissa:
“As if struck by a sword,
As if his head were on fire,
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning sensual lust.”

From: Theragāthā 1.39
